cultivar: Mixed small- and medium-leaf populations related to the Yibang small-leaf type, with ordinary large-leaf trees
processing: Raw pu-erh: pan-fired, hand-rolled and sun-dried maocha, pressed into small-run cakes or sold loose; production is tiny and almost entirely hand-processed by village households.
harvest_season: Spring (late March to April) for the few old-tree lots; autumn tea is sold at lower prices.
appearance_dry: Small to medium dark leaves, neatly twisted, with small buds, pressed loosely.
appearance_wet: Small, tender leaves of mixed sizes, yellow-green, finer than Menghai material.
taste_profile: Fine and fragrant, between Yibang and Mangzhi in style: honey and flowers, a light quick bitterness, mild astringency, a light-to-medium body and a long clean sweetness.

brewing.notes: Rinse once, briefly. Small leaf opens fast; keep the first three steeps short and use porcelain to hold the aroma.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest year and hamlet (Zhibeng, Xinfazhai and neighbouring Mangzhi villages), almost always as small boutique cakes or loose maocha, and only since the mid-2000s revival of the six ancient mountains. Young (1–3 years) it is perfumed and fine, and it gains honey across the 5–12-year window; there is no aged Gedeng market because the mountain produced next to nothing under its own name for most of the twentieth century. Supply is 2008–2025, dry-stored, and because the output is so small, a 'Gedeng' cake in any quantity is more likely to be mixed Xiangming-area tea.
description:
Gedeng is the smallest and least known of the six ancient tea mountains of Xishuangbanna, sitting next to Yibang and Mangzhi in Xiangming township, Mengla County. Qing-era records describe a famous tea king tree on Gedeng that the local people honoured before each harvest; the tree is long gone, and so was most of the mountain's tea for much of the twentieth century, which is why its name is only now creeping back onto wrappers.

The remaining old gardens are scattered through secondary forest at roughly 1,300–1,500 m and include small- and medium-leaf trees of the same family as Yibang's. Everything is hand-processed by a few village households: pan-firing, rolling, sun drying and loose pressing of small batches.

The cup sits between its neighbours: honey and flowers up front, a quick light bitterness, a little astringency, a light-to-medium body and a clean sweetness that lingers. It is less perfumed than Mansong and a little rounder than Yibang old street, with a touch more structure. Flash the early steeps; the small leaf gives everything quickly.

Sold by spring year and hamlet by boutique producers and the Western vendors who visit the area, usually in small cakes or as maocha, at prices that track Yibang. Volumes are tiny, so treat any large or cheap batch as a regional blend of Xiangming-area leaf. It is more a collector's curiosity than a staple, and that is part of its charm.

Taste it as the third tea in a Yibang flight, after old-street Yibang and Mansong, to understand what the six-mountains style has in common.
history:
Gedeng is counted among the six ancient tea mountains of Xishuangbanna, the group on the Mengla side of the Mekong, and is usually described as the least known of them. The usual story tells of a famous tea king tree that was honoured before the harvest, but the details are hazy.

Little is documented about the mountain's tea in the twentieth century. Its name has returned to wrappers only with the modern interest in the six mountains, and output under that name remains small.
